newsitem.title: UK: UK shares set for choppy trading for several weeks.
newsitem.headline: UK shares set for choppy trading for several weeks.

text.p: London investors have had their first serious warning that a stock market correction is due and choppy conditions are possible before the setback occurs, technical analysts said.

The UK stock market as measured by the FTSE 100 index had been storming to record highs for the past several weeks before Friday's sharp retreat and this volatility makes it look increasingly unstable, they say.
By midday Monday, the FTSE had clawed back some of the falls it took on Friday and early Monday to stand down just 28.2 points or 0.58 percent at 4,837.6.
A serious correction could mark the end to the market's strong performance over the past eight months during which the FTSE has charged up over 20 percent.
"This is the first real crack on the equity market," said Luise Kliem, technical analyst at Merrill Lynch.
She said that although the market may hold near the 4,800 level for a few days, investors should brace themselves for a fall to 4,700 with intermediate technical stopping points.

The current high volatility in the market does not preclude a new high to be made -- perhaps to 5,100 -- but the probability of this happening has been diminished following the fallout on Friday, said Kliem.

On Friday, the FTSE had 125 points chopped off as other major markets also went into a tailspin with investors fretting over the instability in the currency markets and possible interest rate hikes in the U.S. and Germany this week.
The lack of breadth in the UK stock market -- with not all stocks within the FTSE having raced up -- should entice investors to switch to the market laggards, analysts said.
"And there are plenty of laggards in the Mid-250 index (of second-line stocks)," said Kliem.

Stocks which have led the FTSE higher have been the banks, pharmaceuticals and oils which have soared by between 25-50 percent compared with electronics, media, and paper groups which have lost four to 15 percent.
Stock market bulls argue that institutional liquidity will allow more money to be pumped into the stock market which will prevent a meltdown.
Current statistics show that UK pension funds on average have 5-1/4 percent of their assets in cash.
"This is high," said Kliem adding some of this money may still be waiting to find a home in the stock market.
"The Mid-250 index held up well on Friday although it looked overbought above 4,600," said Kliem. On Friday the Mid-250 index closed up 8.3 points at 4,692.2.
The index is biased towards the construction, engineering, paper and general retailing stocks which have not been left out of this year's stock market rally.

Nick Glydon, technical analyst at Robert Fleming Securities believes a meltdown is not in prospect but investor attention may now switch to smaller capitalised stocks such as those of the Mid-250 index.
"Much depends on how the Dow reacts and if it can hold on to support at 7,600," said Glydon.

But prospects of disappointing corporate earnings in the U.S. may mean equities on both sides of the Atlantic will head lower towards the end of the year, said Gianpaola Mosconi, bond analyst at Sanwa International.

"The Dow Jones industrials looks overvalued (on the basis of prospective earnings)," said Mosconi, who believes the Dow could fall gradually by up to 10 percent from its peak of about 8,300 as the year progresses and this will hurt equity markets globally.
"For the third quarter we are recommending investors to hold 30 percent of their assets in (global) equities, 40 percent in bonds and 30 percent in cash," said Mosconi.
This is a more conservative asset allocation from that recommended in the first quarter in which 50 percent of investments was advised for global equities, 35 percent in bonds and 15 percent in cash.
"Interest rates in the U.S. could go higher," said Mosconi which will hit equities adding that he expected German interest rates to go up in the second half of the year.
